::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Key answer

**The CCW analysis of the Maringe example carries a small but detectable modelling bias, its 95% CIs under-cover, and its type I error is inflated by about half. The QBA adjustments restore nominal coverage and type I error.** The true CCW effect was set to the observed estimate and the study was replayed `r n0(B)` times on the original `r nrow(bd)` patients; a second set of `r n0(B)` replays checked the case of no surgery effect.

| | CCW as published | CCW + QBA adjustment |
|---|---|---|
| HR, surgery within 6 months vs not (95% CI) | `r hr(cr$est_obs)` (`r ci(cr$ci_lo_obs, cr$ci_hi_obs)`), p = `r f3(cr$p_obs)` | `r hr(cr$est_corr)` (`r ci(cr$ci_lo_corr, cr$ci_hi_corr)`), calibrated p = `r f3(cr$p_calibrated)` |
| Bias, log HR (MC 95% interval) | **`r f3(po$bias)`** (`r bias_ci(po)`) | 0 by construction |
| 95% CI coverage (target 95%) | **`r pct(po$coverage)`** | `r pct(adj("95% CI coverage")$value)` |
| Type I error (target 5%) | **`r pct(pn$reject_0)`** | `r pct(adj("Type I error")$value)` |
| Power at the observed effect | `r pct(po$reject_0)` | `r pct(adj("Power")$value)` |

Monte Carlo SE: about 0.2–0.3 percentage points for coverage and type I error, 0.006 for the bias. Bold cells differ from the target by more than their Monte Carlo error. Adjusted performance is cross-fitted (corrections estimated on one half of the replays, checked on the other).

- **Bias:** the average estimate is HR `r hr(po$mean_est)` instead of `r hr(po$truth)`, slightly too favourable to surgery (`r pct(abs(po$std_bias), 0)` of one SE).
- **Coverage:** the robust SE is `r pct(abs(po$rel_err_modse))` too small, so the CIs cover the truth `r pct(po$coverage)` of the time.
- **Type I error:** with no surgery effect, `r pct(pn$reject_0)` of studies are significant, `r pct(pn$reject_0_lower)` of them in favour of surgery. Even with unlimited data the null CCW HR would be `r hr(truth_table_maringe[scenario == "null", psi_large_sample])`.
- **Conclusion unchanged:** the observed result was not significant (p = `r f3(cr$p_obs)`) and is less so after adjustment (p = `r f3(cr$p_calibrated)`).
:::

**What changed since the 5 October report:** one dataset only (Maringe, as agreed for the paper); `r n0(B)` instead of 5,000 replays per scenario; the censoring mechanism is addressed explicitly (Section 2.3); performance of the adjusted analysis is now evaluated, not only the adjusted estimate. The two-dataset report is kept in `archive/2026-10-05_two_datasets/`. Results agree with that run within Monte Carlo error.

# 1. What was done

The draft paper's steps, applied to the published CCW analysis of Maringe et al. (2020):

| Paper step | What it means here |
|---|---|
| 1. Fit the reference model | Run the CCW analysis on the original data (Section 1.1). |
| 2. Keep baseline data | All covariates **and each patient's actual surgery date** are kept unchanged. |
| 3. Predict outcomes | New death times from a Weibull model fitted to the data, in which surgery changes the hazard **from the day it takes place**. Surgery happens only if the patient is alive on that date. Censoring is predicted as well (Section 2.3). The surgery effect is calibrated so that the true CCW effect equals the observed estimate. |
| 4. Repeat | `r n0(B)` replays per scenario; two scenarios: observed effect and no effect (`r n0(nrow(sim_results_maringe))` CCW analyses; `r n_fail` failed). |
| 5. Re-analyse | The same CCW function as on the real data. |
| 6. Quantify | Bias, CI coverage, type I error and power, each with Monte Carlo SE. |
| 7. Adjust | Bias-corrected estimate, widened CI, calibrated critical value and p-value; their performance checked by cross-fitting. |

## 1.1 Data and analysis

The dataset is the simulated example distributed with Maringe et al. (2020; `ccwr::lungcancer`): `r nrow(bd)` elderly patients with stage I–II lung cancer, followed from diagnosis for one year. `r sum(is.finite(bd$trt_time))` had surgery (`r sum(bd$trt_time <= 1)` on day 1) and `r sum(bd$status)` died. It is not the registry cohort of their Table S2, but the table below uses the same layout.

```{r tab-baseline}
#| tbl-cap: "Patient characteristics by surgery during follow-up."
tb <- copy(table_baseline_maringe)
grp <- attr(table_baseline_maringe, "groups")
tb[indent == 1L, label := paste0("&emsp;", label)]
tb[indent == 0L & label != "", label := paste0("**", label, "**")]
setnames(tb, c("label", "n1", "p1", "n0", "p0", "smd"),
         c("", paste(grp[1], "N"), "%", paste(grp[2], "N"), "% ", "SMD (%)"))
knitr::kable(tb[, -"indent"], align = "lrrrrr", escape = FALSE)
```

| Protocol element | Maringe et al. (2020) |
|---|---|
| Time zero | Cancer diagnosis |
| Strategies | Surgery within 6 months (182.62 days, arm 1) vs no surgery within 6 months (arm 0) |
| Outcome, follow-up | All-cause death; to death or 1 year (365.24 days) |
| Artificial censoring | Arm 0: on the day of surgery (if within 6 months). Arm 1: at 182.62 days if alive and not operated. Deaths before 6 months without surgery count in both arms. |
| Censoring weights | Arm 0: Cox model for time to surgery, weights updated at each surgery date. Arm 1: logistic model for surgery by 6 months among survivors. Both on age, sex, performance status, stage, deprivation, Charlson index, emergency presentation. |
| Outcome model | Weighted Cox, strategy only, Efron ties, robust (patient-clustered) SE |
| Loss to follow-up | None: every survivor is followed to 1 year |

```{r fig-prot}
#| fig-cap: "How example patients are cloned into both strategies, when each clone is artificially censored, and which part of follow-up carries a censoring weight (drawn with the analysis code's own rules). Shaded: grace period."
knitr::include_graphics(fig(targets::tar_read(fig_protocol_maringe, store = store)), error = FALSE)
```

**Covariate balance at 6 months** (as Figure S2 of Maringe et al.). Among clones still at risk at the end of the grace period, the arms differ strongly before weighting; the censoring weights reduce, but do not remove, these differences.

```{r fig-balance}
#| fig-cap: "Standardised differences between the surgery and no-surgery arms among clones at risk at day 182.62, before and after censoring weights. Dashed lines: ±10%."
#| out-width: "75%"
knitr::include_graphics(fig(grep("\\.png$", targets::tar_read(fig_balance_maringe, store = store), value = TRUE)), error = FALSE)
```

```{r balance-text}
bal <- targets::tar_read(balance_maringe, store = store)
bw <- bal[weighting == "Weighted"]
bu <- bal[weighting == "Unweighted"]
over <- bw[abs(smd) > 10][order(-abs(smd))]
lab_b <- c(age_c = "age", sex = "sex", perf0 = "performance status 0", perf1 = "performance status 1",
           perf2 = "performance status 2", stage = "stage", deprivation = "deprivation",
           charlson0 = "Charlson 0", charlson1 = "Charlson 1", charlson2 = "Charlson 2",
           emergency = "emergency presentation")
over_txt <- paste0(lab_b[over$term], " ", formatC(over$smd, format = "f", digits = 1), "%", collapse = ", ")
```

Before weighting, `r sum(abs(bu$smd) > 10)` of `r nrow(bu)` covariate terms differ by more than 10% (largest `r formatC(max(abs(bu$smd)), format = "f", digits = 1)`%); after weighting, `r nrow(over)` still do (`r over_txt`). In the registry data of Maringe et al. all weighted differences were within 10%; in this 200-patient example the weight models leave residual imbalance. This is consistent with the no-effect scenario, where the CCW estimate stays below HR = 1 even with unlimited data (Section 2.2).

## 1.2 Run time

```{r tab-runtime}
#| tbl-cap: "Computing time of the full pipeline by stage (sum over targets, all workers)."
mt <- data.table(meta)
mt[, stage := fcase(
  grepl("^calibration_maringe$", name), "Calibration of θ* (paper Step 3)",
  grepl("^truth_maringe_", name), "True values ψ(θ*) and ψ(0)",
  grepl("^sim_results_maringe_", name), "Simulated studies (paper Steps 3–5)",
  default = "Data, model fits, summaries, tables, figures, report"
)]
n_large_cal <- nrow(cal$path) * cfg$calibration$n_rep
units <- c(
  "Calibration of θ* (paper Step 3)" = n_large_cal,
  "True values ψ(θ*) and ψ(0)" = 2 * cfg$truth$n_rep,
  "Simulated studies (paper Steps 3–5)" = 2 * B
)
unit_lab <- c(
  "Calibration of θ* (paper Step 3)" = "large datasets of 50,000",
  "True values ψ(θ*) and ψ(0)" = "large datasets of 50,000",
  "Simulated studies (paper Steps 3–5)" = "CCW analyses of 200 patients"
)
rt <- mt[, .(seconds = sum(seconds, na.rm = TRUE)), by = stage]
rt[, `:=`(n = units[stage], what = unit_lab[stage])]
rt <- rt[order(-seconds)]
tot <- sum(rt$seconds)
knitr::kable(rt[, .(
  Stage = stage,
  Minutes = formatC(seconds / 60, format = "f", digits = 1),
  `Share` = pct(seconds / tot, 0),
  Units = fifelse(is.na(n), "", paste(n0(n), what)),
  `Seconds per unit` = fifelse(is.na(n), "", formatC(seconds / n, format = "f", digits = 3))
)], align = "lrrlr")
```

```{r runtime-wall}
rs <- targets::tar_read(run_settings, store = store)
# Workers actually used, counted from the timestamps of the simulation branches
source(file.path(root, "R", "utils.R"), local = TRUE)
rs$workers <- observed_workers(mt)
heavy <- mt[grepl("^(calibration|truth|sim_results)_maringe", name)]
# Elapsed time of the simulation stages, from the first start to the last finish
wall <- as.numeric(difftime(max(heavy$time), min(heavy$time - heavy$seconds), units = "mins"))
```

Computing time was `r formatC(tot / 60, format = "f", digits = 1)` minutes; with `r rs$workers` parallel worker`r if (isTRUE(rs$workers > 1)) "s" else ""` (`crew` `r rs$crew`, `r rs$cores` cores available, `r session$platform$version`) the simulation stages took `r formatC(wall, format = "f", digits = 1)` minutes of elapsed time. The `r n0(2 * B / cfg$batch_size)` batches of simulated studies and the two true values run in parallel; the calibration search is sequential because each step needs the previous one, so it sets the lower bound (`r formatC(rt[grepl("^Calibration", stage), seconds] / 60, format = "f", digits = 1)` minutes) however many workers are used. One CCW analysis of the 200 patients takes about `r formatC(1000 * rt[grepl("^Simulated", stage), seconds] / (2 * B), format = "f", digits = 0)` ms; the large datasets that define the true value take `r pct(sum(rt[grepl("^(Calibration|True)", stage), seconds]) / tot, 0)` of the computing time. Results do not depend on the number of workers: every replicate draws from its own seed.

# 2. How the simulation works {#methods}

## 2.1 Simulate patients, not the CCW

CCW is an analysis procedure (cloning, artificial censoring, censoring weights, weighted outcome model), not a model of how outcomes arise, so nothing can be drawn from it directly:

- The fitted CCW outcome model describes survival under two *strategies*: every patient appears in both arms, with one hazard ratio from day 0. A real patient has one history, and before surgery both strategies are identical for that patient.
- The cloned dataset is not data: clones, artificial censoring and weights are produced by the analysis. Redrawing outcomes on the clones with weights held fixed would test only a weighted Cox fit, not CCW.

So the outcome-generating model is a patient-level model fitted to the original data: Weibull survival with surgery as a time-varying exposure, h(t) = h₀(t)·exp(γ′X + θ·1{t ≥ surgery date}). Covariates and surgery dates are kept (paper Step 2) and new death times are drawn. Each simulated dataset looks like the original data, and the whole CCW procedure is re-run on it.

## 2.2 Why the truth is not θ, and calibration

θ is the effect of surgery *once received*, at fixed covariates. The CCW hazard ratio compares *strategies* and differs from θ because of grace-period dilution (in the surgery arm patients are untreated until their surgery date), non-proportional strategy hazards, and non-collapsibility (the CCW model contains the strategy only). None of these has a closed form, so the truth ψ(θ) is computed numerically: the base data are copied to `r n0(ceiling(cfg$truth$n_target / nrow(bd)) * nrow(bd))` patients, outcomes are simulated and the same CCW function is run; this is repeated `r cfg$truth$n_rep` times and averaged.

θ is then searched until ψ(θ) equals the observed CCW estimate (paper Step 3):

```{r tab-calib}
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration path (secant search, 12 large datasets per step)."
p <- copy(cal$path)
knitr::kable(p[, .(Step = step, `θ (log HR)` = f3(theta), `Weibull HR exp(θ)` = hr(theta),
                   `ψ(θ), CCW log HR` = f3(psi), `CCW HR` = hr(psi))], align = "rrrrr")
```

Result: θ\* = `r f3(cal$theta_star)` (Weibull HR `r hr(cal$theta_star)`), against the fitted coefficient θ = `r f3(dm$theta_hat)` (HR `r hr(dm$theta_hat)`). With `r cfg$truth$n_rep` large datasets the truth is ψ(θ\*) = `r f3(po$truth)` (HR `r hr(po$truth)`, MCSE `r f3(po$truth_mcse)`), equal to the observed `r f3(obs$estimate)` within Monte Carlo error. The draft's sentence "θ = −0.70, which results in HR~CCW~ = 0.48" should read: θ\* = −0.70 (Weibull HR `r hr(cal$theta_star)`), which results in HR~CCW~ = `r hr(po$truth)`.

**No-effect scenario (θ = 0).** Every patient's outcome is then identical under both strategies, so every estimand is exactly null and the truth needs no estimation. The large-sample value ψ(0) = `r f3(truth_table_maringe[scenario == "null", psi_large_sample])` is computed only as a diagnostic: it shows that CCW is off-centre even with unlimited data.

## 2.3 Censoring (paper Section 2.3) {#censoring}

The paper says that for time-to-event data the censoring distribution is also predicted, by switching the event/censoring indicator and modelling censoring dependent on covariates, and that the final times are the minimum of event and censoring times. This includes censoring after treatment start.

**How the code does it.** `fit_dgm()` fits a second Weibull model with the indicator switched: loss to follow-up is the event, deaths and the end of follow-up are censored. It uses the same covariates and surgery as a time-varying term, so censoring after treatment start has its own hazard. `simulate_outcomes()` draws a censoring time for each patient by the same inversion as the event time, from its own random numbers, and sets follow-up to min(event, censoring, end of study). This is controlled by `censoring: model` in `config/config.yml` and covered by unit tests.

**Why it changes nothing for Maringe.** In the original data all `r n_surv` survivors are followed to day 365.24: nobody is lost to follow-up. With the indicator switched there are no censoring events, so a censoring model cannot be fitted, and the predicted censoring distribution is the observed one: administrative censoring at one year for every patient. Maringe therefore runs with `censoring: none`, and the simulated data have exactly the original censoring pattern. Artificial censoring of clones is not part of this step: it is produced by the CCW analysis itself in every replay.

**For the paper.** Section 4 should state that the example has administrative censoring only. Two places in the draft disagree with Section 2.3 and could be aligned: the step figure ("keep … censoring times fixed") and Table 1, row "Censoring" ("generated from a separately fitted censoring model"). For Maringe the two descriptions give the same simulated data, because the censoring model reduces to fixed administrative censoring.

# 3. Results

```{r fig-perf}
#| fig-cap: "Bias, 95% CI coverage, type I error and power of the CCW analysis before and after QBA adjustment. Bars: 95% Monte Carlo interval. Dashed: nominal value. The adjusted bias is zero by construction."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(fig_png("fig_performance"), error = FALSE)
```

**Bias.** The average estimate is HR `r hr(po$mean_est)` against a truth of `r hr(po$truth)`: a bias of `r f3(po$bias)` on the log scale (MC 95% interval `r bias_ci(po)`), away from the null, detectable but small (`r pct(abs(po$std_bias), 1)` of one SE).

**Coverage.** The empirical SE is `r f3(po$emp_se)`, the average robust SE `r f3(po$mod_se)` (`r pct(abs(po$rel_err_modse))` too small). Together with the bias this gives coverage of `r pct(po$coverage)` (MCSE `r pct(po$coverage_mcse)`).

**Type I error.** With no surgery effect, `r pct(pn$reject_0)` (MCSE `r pct(pn$reject_0_mcse)`) of studies reject H0: HR = 1 at 5%; `r pct(pn$reject_0_lower)` in favour of surgery and only `r pct(pn$reject_0 - pn$reject_0_lower)` against it. The null estimates are centred at HR `r hr(pn$mean_est)`, of which `r hr(truth_table_maringe[scenario == "null", psi_large_sample])` would remain with unlimited data, most likely because the censoring-weight models do not fully capture how surgery decisions depend on patient characteristics.

**Power** to detect the observed effect is `r pct(po$reject_0)`, consistent with the observed CI that includes 1.

```{r fig-dist}
#| fig-cap: "Left: CCW estimates across replays when the true CCW HR equals the observed estimate. Right: z statistics with no surgery effect, with the nominal (±1.96) and calibrated critical values."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(fig_png("fig_distribution"), error = FALSE)
```

# 4. Adjustment of the observed result (paper Step 7)

```{r tab-corr}
#| tbl-cap: "Observed analysis, calibration and QBA adjustment."
knitr::kable(table_results_maringe$analysis, col.names = c("", "Value"), align = "lr")
```

- **Estimate:** observed − bias, the paper's grid search to first order.
- **CI:** widened by empirical SE / model SE = `r f2(cr$se_inflation)`.
- **Test:** a 5% test needs |z| > `r f2(cr$z_crit_calibrated)` instead of 1.96; the calibrated p-value is the share of no-effect replays with |z| at least as large as observed.

**Does the adjusted analysis work?** Applying the adjustments estimated from half of the replays to the other half: coverage `r pct(adj("95% CI coverage")$value)` (MCSE `r pct(adj("95% CI coverage")$mcse)`), type I error `r pct(adj("Type I error")$value)` (MCSE `r pct(adj("Type I error")$mcse)`). Both are back at their targets. The price is lower power (`r pct(adj("Power")$value)` instead of `r pct(po$reject_0)`), because part of the original power came from the inflated type I error.

```{r tab-perf}
#| tbl-cap: "Performance before and after QBA adjustment (estimate (MCSE))."
knitr::kable(table_results_maringe$performance,
             col.names = c("Performance measure", "CCW as published", "CCW + QBA adjustment"),
             align = "lrr")
```

# 5. Alignment with the draft paper (version 0.62, 8 Oct) {#alignment}

| Draft paper | This run |
|---|---|
| Section 2.3: censoring predicted by switching the event/censoring indicator | **Implemented**; for Maringe it reduces to administrative censoring at 1 year (Section 2.3 above). Step figure and Table 1 "Censoring" row to be aligned. |
| Section 4.2: covariates age, sex, performance status, stage, deprivation, Charlson, emergency | **As used** in both the weight models and the Weibull model. |
| Section 4.3: "θ = −0.70, which results in HR~CCW~ = 0.48" | θ\* = `r f2(cal$theta_star)` is confirmed; HR~CCW~ = `r hr(po$truth)` (= observed), exp(θ\*) = `r hr(cal$theta_star)`. |
| Discussion: "small but detectable bias … type I error rate (7.1%) and 95% CI coverage (93.7%)" | Bias confirmed (`r f3(po$bias)`); coverage **`r pct(po$coverage)`**; type I error **`r pct(pn$reject_0)`**, not 7.1%. |
| Discussion: "QBA-based adjustments successfully restored unbiasedness, the nominal type I error rate, and nominal 95% CI coverage" | **Confirmed** by cross-fitting: coverage `r pct(adj("95% CI coverage")$value)`, type I error `r pct(adj("Type I error")$value)`. |
| Section 4 placeholder: "Report also running time on how many cores" | `r formatC(wall, format = "f", digits = 1)` minutes elapsed with `r rs$workers` worker`r if (isTRUE(rs$workers > 1)) "s" else ""` (`r formatC(tot / 60, format = "f", digits = 1)` minutes of computing time; Section 1.2). |
| ISPE 2026 remark (Wang, Zivich et al.): CCW may have low CI coverage | **Supported:** `r pct(po$coverage)`. |

# 6. Caveats and next steps

- Truths are simulated (MCSE `r f3(po$truth_mcse)`); this is included in the bias interval.
- Adjusted bias is zero by construction under two-fold cross-fitting; coverage and type I error of the adjusted analysis are genuine checks.
- The null offset (ψ(0) ≠ 0) suggests the censoring-weight models are not flexible enough; a sensitivity analysis with splines for age and deprivation in the weight models would test this.
- The Word draft of paper Section 4 (`reports/paper/section4_draft.docx`) uses the same results.

# Appendix

## A1. Performance in both scenarios

```{r tab-perf-all}
tab <- performance_maringe[, .(
  Scenario = c(observed = "Observed effect", null = "No effect")[scenario],
  `θ (DGM)` = f2(theta), `True HR` = hr(truth), `Mean HR` = hr(mean_est),
  `Bias (log HR)` = f3(bias), MCSE = f3(bias_mcse_total),
  `Emp. SE` = f3(emp_se), `Model SE` = f3(mod_se),
  Coverage = pct(coverage), `Reject HR = 1` = pct(reject_0),
  `Mean deaths` = formatC(mean_outcomes, format = "f", digits = 1), Failed = n_fail
)]
knitr::kable(tab, align = "lrrrrrrrrrrr")
```

Measures were cross-checked with `rsimsum` (identical bias, empirical SE, coverage and rejection rate).

## A2. Data-generating mechanism

**Kept fixed from the original data (paper Step 2):** covariates $X_i$ and each patient's surgery date $s_i$ ($s_i = \infty$ if not operated). **Censoring:** $C_i = 365.24$ for all patients (no loss to follow-up; Section 2.3).

**Outcome model.** Weibull proportional hazards with surgery as a time-varying exposure:

$$h_i(t) = \lambda \rho\, t^{\rho - 1} \exp\{\gamma^\top X_i + \theta\, I(t \ge s_i)\}, \qquad \eta_i = \log\lambda + \gamma^\top X_i,$$

$$H_i(t) = e^{\eta_i}\left[\min(t, s_i)^{\rho} + e^{\theta}\,\max\{0,\; t^{\rho} - s_i^{\rho}\}\right].$$

Fitted by maximum likelihood, $\ell = \sum_i \left[\delta_i \log h_i(Y_i) - H_i(Y_i)\right]$ (Table A2). In simulation, $\log\lambda$, $\rho$ and $\gamma$ are kept at their fitted values and $\theta$ is set to the scenario value ($\theta^*$ or 0). Where a censoring model is fitted, it has the same form with the indicator switched ($1 - \delta_i$ for loss to follow-up).

**Simulation by inversion** (common random numbers: $U_i$ depends only on the replicate seed, not on $\theta$). With $E_i = -\log U_i$:

$$T_i = \begin{cases} \left(E_i\, e^{-\eta_i}\right)^{1/\rho} & \text{if } E_i \le e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho} \text{ (death before surgery)},\\[4pt] \left\{ s_i^{\rho} + \left(E_i - e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho}\right) e^{-\eta_i - \theta} \right\}^{1/\rho} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

**Observed data:** $Y_i = \min(T_i, C_i)$, $\delta_i = I(T_i \le C_i)$; surgery is observed at $s_i$ only if $s_i \le Y_i$.

## A3. Censoring weights and outcome model

Grace period $g = 182.62$ days; $Z$ = age, sex, performance status, stage, deprivation, Charlson index, emergency presentation.

- *Arm 0, no surgery within $g$.* Censored at surgery: $C^a_i = s_i$ if $s_i \le \min(g, Y_i)$. Cox model for time to surgery with Breslow baseline; weights updated at every distinct surgery date:
$$W_i(t) = \frac{1}{\hat S^c(t \mid Z_i)} = \exp\left\{\hat\Lambda^c_0\big(\min(t, g)\big)\, e^{\hat\beta^\top Z_i}\right\}.$$
- *Arm 1, surgery within $g$.* Censored at $g$ if alive and not operated. Logistic model among patients alive at $g$, $\pi(Z) = P(s \le g \mid Z, Y > g)$:
$$W_i(t) = 1 \text{ for } t < g, \qquad W_i(t) = 1/\hat\pi(Z_i) \text{ for } t \ge g.$$
- *Outcome model.* Weighted Cox model on the stacked clones, $\lambda(t \mid A) = \lambda_0(t)\, e^{\psi A}$, Efron ties, robust SE clustered on patient, Wald 95% CI.

## A4. True value, calibration, performance and adjustment

- **Truth:** $\tilde\psi(\theta) = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} \hat\psi^{(r)}_N$, with $N = `r n0(ceiling(cfg$truth$n_target / nrow(bd)) * nrow(bd))`$ and $R = `r cfg$truth$n_rep`$.
- **Calibration:** $\theta^*$ solves $\tilde\psi(\theta) = \hat\psi_{\text{obs}}$ (secant search from $\hat\theta$, `r cfg$calibration$n_rep` large datasets per step, tolerance `r cfg$calibration$tol`).
- **Performance** over $B = `r n0(B)`$ replicates: bias $= \bar{\hat\psi} - \psi$; coverage $= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b - \psi| \le 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b)$; rejection rate $= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b| > 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b)$. The MCSE of the bias includes the truth's MC error.
- **Adjustment:** $\hat\psi^{adj} = \hat\psi - \widehat{\text{bias}}$; CI $\hat\psi^{adj} \pm 1.96\, k\, \widehat{SE}$ with $k = \max(1, SE_{emp}/SE_{mod})$; critical value $z^*$ = 95th percentile of $|z|$ under $\theta = 0$. Two-fold cross-fitting over replicate index for the adjusted performance.
